summary: The narrator recounts the aftermath of a press conference for the Xnet movement, which the press and media largely cast as terrorism or terrorist sympathy. Fox News dubbed them "Cal-Quaeda," anti-war leaders disowned them, and the DHS doubled security in San Francisco, frisking the narrator several times a day. Meanwhile the DHS announced nightly arrests of alleged Xnet "ringleaders" and "operatives." The narrator, who was suspended from school and avoided arrest, feels he has failed and is reluctant to blog about the coverage.
one_line: Narrator reflects on a failed Xnet press conference, hostile media coverage calling them terrorists, and DHS crackdowns and arrests in San Francisco.
key_facts: The narrator thought over a press conference the night of the movie, and fell asleep proud of how the big-shot journalists had listened to him.
The narrator's mom asked about the movie and he gave a response he had worked out in advance, cribbed from a review in the Bay Guardian.
Everyone sent the narrator articles to blog, but he did not want to, believing he had blown it.
The press concluded that the Xnet group were terrorists or terrorist dupes.
A Fox News reporter devoted a ten-minute commentary to the group, describing their "criminal treason."
The Fox News reporter named the group "Cal-Quaeda" and called them "spoiled children" who do the terrorists' work on the home front.
Leaders of the anti-war movement denounced the group as fringe elements.
One anti-war figure said the group had been fabricated by the DHS to discredit the anti-war movement.
The DHS announced it would double security in San Francisco.
The DHS demonstrated an arphid cloner it had found, using it to stage a car-theft.
The DHS warned residents to watch for young people behaving suspiciously, especially those whose hands were out of sight.
The narrator finished a paper on Kerouac and started one on the Summer of Love of 1967, when the anti-war movement and hippies converged on San Francisco.
By the end of the week the narrator was frisked an average of four times a day.
Police checked the narrator's ID and questioned him, eyeballing a letter from Chavez saying he was suspended.
The narrator was not arrested, but other Xnet members were.
Each night the DHS announced more arrests of alleged Xnet "ringleaders" and "operatives," paraded on TV with arphid sniffers and other devices.
